headline: New AI Helper Called Hark Promises to Protect Your Privacy While Doing Your Digital Chores

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A company called Hark just made a new computer helper called Hark Pro. It uses artificial intelligence, or AI, which means a computer program that can think and make decisions almost like a person. Hark Pro can do jobs on your computer for you, like answering emails, approving money requests, or even booking a plane ticket. The people who made it say they are different from other big companies because they do not want to use your personal information to sell ads. When Hark Pro does something on the internet, it shows you a little window so you can watch what it is doing. This helps people trust it more. The company that made Hark is run by a man named Brett Adcock. The team also plans to build a brand new kind of gadget by 2027 to go along with the program, though they have not said exactly what it will look like. This matters because more and more companies are trying to build AI helpers, and people want ones that keep their information safe.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: A startup called Hark just released a new AI assistant named Hark Pro that is meant to handle digital tasks for you, like replying to emails, approving expenses, or booking travel. Unlike a regular chatbot that just answers questions, Hark Pro can actually use your computer the way you would, clicking through websites to get things done. To do this, it needs access to parts of your digital life, such as your email, calendar, and even credit card information. The company's leaders say their main goal is different from giant tech companies like Meta or OpenAI. They claim they are not trying to build super-intelligent AI or collect your data to sell ads, just to make a helpful tool. One interesting design choice is that Hark Pro shows users a small window of what it is doing online in real time, instead of hiding the process, so people can trust that it is behaving correctly. A designer named Abidur Chowdhury, who used to work at Apple, says Hark Pro works better than competitors because it finishes tasks completely instead of stopping partway and asking the user to take over. Hark also has bigger plans: by 2027, they want to release a brand-new type of device to go along with the software, though they have not revealed what it looks like. This story matters because companies are racing to create AI assistants people will depend on every day, and privacy is becoming a major selling point in that race.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Tech companies have been experimenting for a while with AI personal assistants, trying to find the right design that makes people actually want to use one every day. Hark, a startup less than a year old, just released its version called Hark Pro, which is free to use with a paid option for people who need more features. Instead of being just a chatbot that answers questions, Hark Pro is built to literally operate a computer on the user's behalf, handling things like approving expenses, replying to emails, and booking flights. To work this well, it needs permission to access someone's email, calendar, and financial accounts, which raises real questions about cybersecurity and how much personal information people are willing to hand over to an AI system. Hark's team argues that they are intentionally different from giant companies like Meta or OpenAI, insisting they are not interested in using people's data to sell advertisements. A designer at Hark named Abidur Chowdhury, formerly of Apple, explained that the assistant tries to build trust by showing users a visible window of its actions as it browses the web, rather than working invisibly behind the scenes like many competitors. He also claims Hark Pro's advantage isn't necessarily speed, but that it finishes tasks completely instead of stopping and asking the user to take over partway through, which many similar apps do. One challenge the article points out is that people often struggle to think of useful tasks to actually hand off to an AI assistant, even when the technology is capable of helping. Looking ahead, Hark plans to release a new kind of physical device by 2027 to work alongside its software, though details are still a secret. This story is worth paying attention to because it shows how the tech industry is competing not just on how smart an AI is, but on how much people can trust it with their most personal information.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: The race to create a must-have AI personal assistant is heating up, with multiple companies releasing competing products trying to find the right combination of usefulness and trust. Hark, a startup founded less than a year ago by entrepreneur Brett Adcock, entered this race with the wide release of Hark Pro, a free app with a paid subscription tier for heavier users. Rather than positioning itself as building artificial general intelligence (AGI, meaning AI as capable as a human across many tasks) or solving massive scientific problems, Hark describes its mission more modestly: creating a usable interface between people and AI. Its model is specifically trained for 'computer use,' meaning it can navigate websites and software the way a human would, handling tasks such as approving expenses, drafting email replies, and booking travel. To function this way, users must grant it access to sensitive parts of their digital lives, including email, calendars, and payment information, which raises legitimate cybersecurity concerns and questions about how much personal data should be entrusted to any single company. Hark's leadership, including designer Abidur Chowdhury (formerly of Apple), frames the company's identity partly around not being like Meta or OpenAI, arguing they aren't interested in selling ads or mining personal data, just completing tasks. However, Chowdhury's own explanation of how the system learns about users — understanding their needs to be more helpful — shows the line between helpfulness and data-driven profiling can be blurry, even with good intentions. One distinctive design decision is letting users see, in a small on-screen window, exactly how the AI navigates the internet to complete a task, rather than hiding that process, which the company hopes will build user trust and transparency. Chowdhury argues Hark Pro's advantage over other options isn't necessarily raw speed, but that it tends to complete tasks fully instead of requiring the user to step in partway through, which he says happens frequently with rival products. A broader unresolved question raised in the article is whether a model trained narrowly for computer navigation tasks sacrifices some of the deeper reasoning ability found in general-purpose, frontier language models. Looking forward, Hark has also promised an entirely new kind of AI-native hardware device by 2027, intended to work alongside the software, though the company has stayed vague about its form, with Chowdhury expressing a conscious desire to avoid 'creepy' wearable technology like cameras. Whether this becomes a genuinely novel product or just another repackaged gadget remains an open question the public will have to wait to answer.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: As tech companies continue chasing the elusive formula for an AI personal assistant people can't live without, a new entrant called Hark has released its product, Hark Pro, into an increasingly crowded field. Founded less than a year ago by serial entrepreneur Brett Adcock, Hark distinguishes itself not by claiming to build artificial general intelligence or solve grand scientific challenges, but by positioning itself more humbly as a user interface layer for AI — essentially, an operating system designed for a future generation of AI-driven computers. Its underlying model is trained specifically for 'computer use,' meaning it is optimized to navigate digital interfaces and complete tasks autonomously, such as approving expense reports, responding to emails, and booking travel, rather than simply answering conversational questions like a typical chatbot. Functionally, this requires deep access to a user's digital infrastructure: email accounts, calendars, hard drives, and even financial information, which naturally invites scrutiny around cybersecurity risk and the broader question of how comfortable users should be entrusting so much personal data to a single third-party system. This is where Hark's branding leans heavily into differentiation from dominant players like Meta and OpenAI, with design lead Abidur Chowdhury (a former Apple designer) explicitly stating the company has no interest in monetizing user data through advertising. Yet his own description of the system — that it works to 'understand' users in order to be more helpful — illustrates the inherent tension in this kind of product: even assistants built with privacy-forward intentions must build detailed behavioral profiles of users and the people in their lives to function effectively, and reassurances about intent don't necessarily eliminate structural privacy risk. One notable design decision intended to address user trust is a visible interface window showing exactly how the AI agent navigates websites in real time, a transparency feature most competing AI assistants don't offer, since they typically perform such actions invisibly. Chowdhury contends that Hark Pro's edge over rivals, such as the AI assistant Muse, isn't necessarily processing speed but reliability: the ability to complete tasks fully and autonomously rather than pausing midway and requiring human intervention, a common limitation of competing products. The article also highlights a subtler challenge facing this entire product category: users often struggle to identify genuinely useful tasks to delegate to an AI, even when the underlying technology is technically capable, suggesting that adoption hurdles may be as much about imagination and habit as about raw capability. Additionally, there's an unresolved technical trade-off worth considering: a model narrowly trained for computer navigation may sacrifice some of the broader reasoning and knowledge depth found in general-purpose 'frontier' language models, raising questions about long-term versatility versus short-term task efficiency. Beyond software, Hark has signaled ambitions toward hardware, promising an entirely new category of AI-native device by 2027, though specifics remain deliberately vague, with Chowdhury expressing reluctance toward surveillance-adjacent wearables like cameras due to their 'creep factor.' Ultimately, this story captures a pivotal moment in the broader AI industry: a shift from assistants that merely answer questions toward autonomous agents that act on users' behalf, and the accompanying societal negotiation over how much trust, access, and oversight such systems should be granted.

questions: If an AI assistant needed access to your email, calendar, and financial accounts to work well, how would you decide whether that trade-off was worth it?

Hark says it wants to build trust by showing users how it navigates the web — do you think seeing an AI's actions really makes it more trustworthy, or could it just make people feel safer without changing what's really happening?
As AI assistants become more common in homes and schools, what rules or limits do you think should exist to protect people's privacy, especially for kids and teens?
